subtopic_detail: the hypnotic itself as the cause of a fall in an older woman, and how to stop it without simply substituting another sedative
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 78 year old woman two weeks after she fell getting up to the toilet at three in the morning and fractured her left wrist. She has taken zopiclone 7.5 mg nightly for the past four years, started after her husband died.

She says the tablet no longer works as it once did and that she often feels foggy for an hour or two after waking. She lives alone in a single storey home, uses no walking aid, and her postural blood pressure, visual acuity and gait speed have all been checked and were normal. Her vitamin D and calcium are adequate and she is on a bisphosphonate. She has no other sedating medication, drinks no alcohol, and her cognitive screening score is normal. She is frightened of both falling again and of lying awake all night.

data_table.Examination: Left wrist in a cast, timed up and go test 10 seconds, no postural drop, Mini Mental State Examination 29 of 30
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea electrolytes and creatinine, thyroid stimulating hormone and corrected calcium all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her insomnia?

options.text: Substitute temazepam 10 mg at night as a safer hypnotic alternative
options.rationale: Temazepam carries the same fall, fracture and cognitive risks in older people as the non benzodiazepine hypnotics and appears on the same list of drugs to avoid in this age group, so the substitution changes the molecule without changing the hazard. Swapping between agents in the same class is a common way of appearing to act while leaving the risk in place. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Cease the zopiclone tonight and advise that any rebound will settle
options.rationale: Abrupt withdrawal after four years of nightly use produces rebound insomnia and anxiety severe enough that most patients restart within days, and withdrawal seizures are described with hypnotics of this class. The direction is right but the rate is unsafe and self defeating. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Taper the zopiclone gradually alongside cognitive behavioural therapy
options.rationale: A planned dose reduction over weeks to months, paired with cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, achieves durable cessation in a substantial proportion of long term users and gives her a treatment for the sleep problem rather than only removing the drug. Offering the therapy at the same time as the taper is what makes her able to accept it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Add prolonged release melatonin and continue her usual zopiclone dose
options.rationale: Prolonged release melatonin is a reasonable option in people over 55 and is useful as a bridge during a taper, but adding it while the hypnotic continues leaves her on the drug that is most likely to have caused the fall. It is an adjunct to withdrawal, not a reason to defer it. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Continue the zopiclone given her normal gait and vision assessments
options.rationale: A normal gait, normal postural blood pressure and normal vision do not neutralise the risk, they leave the sedative as the only modifiable contributor identified, and the fall occurred in the middle of the night when the drug effect is maximal. Continuing is the option that ignores the disconfirming negative workup. (Source: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine)
source_refs: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine

explanation.summary: Sedative hypnotics roughly double the risk of falls and hip fracture in older people, and the risk is present with the non benzodiazepine agents as much as with benzodiazepines despite the marketing distinction between them. A fall at night in someone taking a nightly hypnotic should prompt a medication review before an extensive falls workup, and a negative workup strengthens rather than weakens the case for deprescribing. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is the first line treatment for chronic insomnia at any age and its benefits outlast those of drug treatment, which is why it is offered as the replacement rather than as an afterthought. Tapering works best when the patient understands that rebound insomnia is expected, time limited and not evidence that the drug was necessary. Australian programs that combine a patient information leaflet with a planned taper achieve cessation rates well above usual care.
key_points: Non benzodiazepine hypnotics carry the same fall and fracture risk as benzodiazepines in older people
A night time fall in a hypnotic user points to the drug before it points to the gait
Switching within the sedative class does not reduce risk
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia outlasts drug treatment and is first line
Warn about expected rebound insomnia so it is not misread as relapse
explanation.pearls: Reduce the hypnotic by about one quarter of the original dose every one to two weeks, and expect rebound insomnia to peak in the first three to five nights after each reduction and settle within one to two weeks.

sources.label: Australian and New Zealand Society for Geriatric Medicine

subtopic_detail: new self directed hitting and food refusal in a non speaking adult with intellectual disability whose environment has not changed
stem:
You are the registrar in a community disability health service asked to see a 34 year old man with severe intellectual disability who does not use speech. Over the past three weeks he has begun hitting the side of his own head with an open hand, mostly in the evenings, and has become resistant at mealtimes.

His support workers report that his house, staff roster, day program and routine are all unchanged, and that no new medication has been started. He is still drinking his usual fluids and will accept yoghurt and soup, but pushes away the toast and apple he previously ate every day. He has lost 2 kg in three weeks. He is afebrile and his bowels are opening daily. The behaviour support practitioner has asked you to prescribe something to settle him before a functional assessment can be scheduled.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, blood pressure 126/78, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 98 per cent in air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Resists approach to the face, no external swelling, chest and abdomen unremarkable, no guarding
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea electrolytes and creatinine, C reactive protein and thyroid stimulating hormone all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence risperidone at low dose and review the behaviour in two weeks
options.rationale: Prescribing an antipsychotic for behaviour in intellectual disability before a physical cause has been excluded is the central anti pattern in this population and produces sedation, weight gain and a masked underlying illness. It has a place only once medical and environmental causes have been addressed and a behaviour support plan has failed. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Refer for a functional behaviour assessment and await its recommendations
options.rationale: Functional assessment is a core part of management but is designed to analyse the environmental antecedents and consequences of behaviour, and it will not identify an untreated physical cause. Deferring to it here delays the examination that the pattern of the presentation is pointing toward. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Commence sertraline for a presumed underlying depressive presentation
options.rationale: Depression does present atypically in people who do not use speech and can show as behaviour change and reduced intake, but the selective refusal of hard foods while soft foods are accepted is a mechanical pattern rather than a loss of appetite. An antidepressant would be considered after a physical cause is excluded and the picture remained pervasive. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Undertake a systematic physical examination including the mouth and ears
options.rationale: New behaviour in a person who cannot report symptoms is treated as pain or illness until proven otherwise, and the combination of self directed hitting at one site, refusal of foods that require chewing and preserved fluid intake points to an examination of the teeth, jaw and ears. Dental disease and otitis media are among the most frequently missed causes in this group. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Start regular paracetamol and reassess the behaviour after one week
options.rationale: A trial of simple analgesia is a defensible step when pain is suspected but no source is found, and here the examination has not yet been done, so treating blindly risks partially masking a treatable infection. Analgesia belongs alongside a diagnosis rather than instead of looking for one. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Diagnostic overshadowing is the tendency to attribute new symptoms in a person with intellectual disability to the disability itself rather than to an independent illness, and it is one of the main drivers of avoidable deaths in this population. People who do not use speech communicate pain through behaviour, so a change in behaviour carries the same weight as a new symptom would in anyone else. The commonest missed causes are dental disease, constipation, gastro oesophageal reflux, urinary tract infection, otitis media, fracture and epilepsy related phenomena. The pattern of the behaviour often localises the problem: hitting one side of the head, refusing foods that need chewing, or a new stoop while transferring each point somewhere. Australian practice standards require that physical causes be excluded and that psychotropic medication for behaviour be time limited with a planned review, because this group is heavily over prescribed antipsychotics.
key_points: Treat new behaviour in a non speaking adult as pain or illness until excluded
Selective refusal of hard foods with preserved fluids is a mechanical pattern, not anorexia
Normal inflammatory markers do not exclude dental abscess or dental caries
Functional behaviour assessment analyses environment and will not find a physical cause
Antipsychotics prescribed for behaviour need an explicit indication, a target and a review date
explanation.pearls: An unchanged environment makes an environmental trigger much less likely and shifts the odds decisively toward a physical cause, which is why asking about roster, housemate and routine changes is part of the medical assessment rather than the behavioural one.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: recurrent winter depressive episodes with oversleeping and carbohydrate craving that remit each spring in a high latitude Australian city
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 31 year old woman in Hobart in mid July. For the third consecutive year she has become flat, unmotivated and tearful from about May onward.

She sleeps ten to eleven hours and still wakes unrefreshed, craves bread and sweet food, and has gained 5 kg since April. She finds it hardest in the first hours of the day. Each of the two previous episodes lifted completely in September without treatment and she was fully well through summer, working and socialising normally. She has never had a period of elevated mood, reduced need for sleep or overspending. Her thyroid function, ferritin and vitamin D have been checked this month and are normal, and she has no thoughts of self harm.

data_table.Examination: Slowed but reactive, no psychomotor retardation on formal testing, weight 74 kg
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone, ferritin, vitamin D and full blood count all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first treatment?

options.text: Commence fluoxetine 20 mg each morning and review her again in four weeks
options.rationale: A serotonergic antidepressant is an effective treatment for this pattern of depression and is a legitimate alternative, but it is not preferred ahead of a treatment with an equivalent effect size, a faster onset and no systemic adverse effects. It becomes the choice if the first line treatment is declined, poorly tolerated or ineffective. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Prescribe high dose colecalciferol weekly and reassess her mood in a month
options.rationale: Vitamin D deficiency is common at this latitude in winter and worth correcting when present, but hers has been measured this month and is normal, so supplementation has no target. Trials of vitamin D for depression have not shown benefit in people who are already replete. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Arrange bright light therapy for thirty minutes soon after waking each day
options.rationale: Daily morning exposure to a 10 000 lux light box is the first line treatment for a depressive episode with a seasonal pattern, with response rates comparable to antidepressants and a typical onset within one to two weeks. Morning timing is the active ingredient because it advances the delayed circadian phase that underlies the oversleeping and morning worsening. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Start agomelatine at night with liver function testing before and during
options.rationale: Agomelatine acts on melatonergic receptors and has a rational circadian mechanism, but it is a later line agent in Australian practice and requires liver function monitoring before treatment and at intervals through the first five months. There is no reason to accept that monitoring burden ahead of a non pharmacological first line option. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Begin lithium augmentation given the recurrent and periodic course she has
options.rationale: A periodic recurrent course raises the question of bipolarity, but she has never had a hypomanic or manic period and a seasonal unipolar pattern is not itself an indication for a mood stabiliser. Lithium augmentation is a strategy for treatment resistant depression, and she has had no treatment yet. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: A seasonal pattern is a specifier applied to recurrent major depressive disorder when episodes begin and remit at characteristic times of year across at least two consecutive years, with full remission in between and with seasonal episodes substantially outnumbering non seasonal ones. The winter pattern characteristically shows atypical or reversed neurovegetative features, meaning hypersomnia, increased appetite with carbohydrate craving and weight gain, which is the opposite of the classic melancholic picture. Prevalence rises with latitude, so the pattern is more often seen in Tasmania and southern Victoria than in Queensland. The differential includes hypothyroidism, iron deficiency and vitamin D deficiency, all of which are more prevalent in winter and all of which should be measured before the diagnosis is settled. Preventive light therapy started before the usual month of onset is an option for people with a highly predictable pattern.
key_points: Two consecutive years of seasonal onset and remission are required for the specifier
Winter pattern episodes typically show hypersomnia and carbohydrate craving rather than insomnia and weight loss
Bright light at 10 000 lux for about 30 minutes shortly after waking is first line
Check thyroid function, ferritin and vitamin D before settling on the diagnosis
Screen for a history of hypomania before treating any highly recurrent depression
explanation.pearls: Light therapy works only if the eyes receive the light, so the box sits at about an arm's length in the upper visual field while the person reads or eats breakfast, and response is usually apparent within one to two weeks rather than the four to six expected of an antidepressant.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: choosing between magnetic stimulation and electroconvulsive therapy after two failed antidepressant trials in a patient who is eating and not suicidal
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 45 year old plumber with a current major depressive episode of fourteen months. He completed twelve weeks of escitalopram 20 mg daily and then ten weeks of venlafaxine 225 mg daily, both taken as prescribed, with no meaningful change.

He has also had sixteen sessions of cognitive behavioural therapy. He is eating and drinking normally, has lost no weight, and continues to work three days a week although he says he is going through the motions. He denies any intent to end his life and has made no plans. He holds no delusional beliefs about guilt, illness or poverty, and there is no stupor, mutism or waxy flexibility. He has never had a seizure and takes no other medication.

data_table.Examination: Reduced spontaneous speech, reactive affect, no psychomotor retardation, cognition intact
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, urea electrolytes and creatinine, liver function tests and thyroid stimulating hormone all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next treatment?

options.text: Switch to a third antidepressant from a different pharmacological class
options.rationale: Remission rates fall substantially with each successive antidepressant switch, and after two adequate trials the yield from a third is low enough that guidelines move to augmentation or a neurostimulation treatment. A further switch would postpone an effective option by another three months. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange an urgent course of electroconvulsive therapy under anaesthesia
options.rationale: Electroconvulsive therapy is the most effective treatment available and is the right choice for depression with psychotic features, catatonia, food and fluid refusal or high imminent suicide risk, none of which is present. Choosing it here means accepting general anaesthesia and cognitive adverse effects when a less burdensome option has not been tried. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

options.text: Refer for a course of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation
options.rationale: This is the treatment positioned for a moderate depressive episode that has failed two adequate antidepressant trials in a patient who is physically well and not at imminent risk, and in Australia it attracts a Medicare rebate at exactly this point in the sequence. It is given awake without anaesthesia and does not carry the cognitive burden of the seizure based treatment. (Source: Medicare Benefits Schedule Australia)

options.text: Augment the venlafaxine with lithium and monitor levels and renal function
options.rationale: Lithium augmentation is an evidence based strategy at this stage and is a genuine competitor, but it requires ongoing level monitoring, renal and thyroid surveillance, and carries a narrow therapeutic index in a man who works with machinery and tools. It remains a reasonable option if the neurostimulation course does not achieve remission. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence a course of intravenous ketamine infusions in a day unit setting
options.rationale: Ketamine and esketamine produce rapid reductions in depressive symptoms and are most useful where speed matters, such as acute suicidality, which is not the situation here, and access in Australia is limited and largely unsubsidised. Its antidepressant effect also wanes within days to weeks without repeated dosing. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

explanation.summary: Treatment resistant depression is conventionally defined as failure to respond to two antidepressants given at an adequate dose for an adequate duration with confirmed adherence, and establishing that those two trials really were adequate is the first task rather than a formality. Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation delivers focal magnetic pulses to the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex over a course of around twenty to thirty sessions on consecutive weekdays, without anaesthesia and without inducing a seizure. Australian Medicare subsidy became available in 2021 for an initial course in adults with a diagnosed major depressive episode who have failed two adequate trials, which makes the two trial threshold a practical as well as a clinical cut off. Electroconvulsive therapy remains more effective overall and stays the treatment of choice where the illness is life threatening or psychotic. Ordering these options wrongly either exposes a well patient to anaesthesia or leaves a severely ill one waiting weeks for a slower treatment.
key_points: Confirm dose adequacy, duration and adherence before labelling a trial as failed
Two adequate failed trials is the Australian threshold for subsidised magnetic stimulation
Psychosis, catatonia, food refusal or imminent suicide risk move the choice to electroconvulsive therapy
Magnetic stimulation is given awake, on consecutive weekdays, over four to six weeks
Lithium augmentation remains a valid alternative at the same point in the sequence
explanation.pearls: The seizure threshold matters in opposite directions for the two treatments: electroconvulsive therapy deliberately induces a seizure, whereas an inadvertent seizure is the principal serious adverse event of magnetic stimulation, so concurrent bupropion, tramadol or clozapine must be identified before a course begins.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists

subtopic_detail: repugnant intrusive images of harming a newborn with preserved insight and checking behaviour, seven weeks after birth
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 29 year old woman at her baby's seven week check. She asks to speak to you alone and then, with great difficulty, tells you that pictures keep coming into her mind of the baby slipping from her arms on the stairs and of a knife.

She describes the images as horrible and says they make her feel sick. She has started carrying the baby only on the ground floor, has moved the kitchen knives to a high cupboard, and checks the baby's breathing eight or nine times a night. She says she would never do any of it and that she cannot understand why her mind produces it. She is sleeping when the baby sleeps, is feeding the baby well and is delighted by him when he smiles. She is fully oriented, hears nothing others cannot hear, and holds no beliefs that the baby is abnormal or in danger from others.

data_table.Examination: Anxious and ashamed, fully oriented, no perceptual abnormality, warm and attuned interaction with the infant
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone, full blood count and ferritin all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange urgent admission to a mother and baby unit for further observation
options.rationale: Admission is indicated for postpartum psychosis or for severe depression with impaired capacity to care for the infant, and the discriminating features of psychosis are absent: she is oriented, has no perceptual disturbance and holds no delusional beliefs about the baby. Hospitalising an egodystonic obsessional presentation amplifies the shame that already delayed her disclosure. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence Australia)

options.text: Notify child protection services and arrange supervised contact meanwhile
options.rationale: Intrusive thoughts of harm that are unwanted and repugnant to the mother carry no increased risk of harm to the infant, and the risk in this presentation runs the other way, toward mothers concealing symptoms because they fear exactly this response. Reporting would be warranted if the thoughts were ego syntonic or accompanied by delusional beliefs about the child. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence Australia)

options.text: Commence olanzapine at night and review her in the surgery within a week
options.rationale: An antipsychotic treats the psychotic presentation this is being mistaken for and does nothing for obsessional symptoms, while adding sedation to a woman caring for a newborn overnight. The distinction that determines the drug class is whether the thoughts are recognised as the mind's own product, which she states clearly. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention
options.rationale: Perinatal obsessive compulsive disorder responds to the same therapy as at other times, targeting the avoidance of the stairs and knives and the repeated checking that maintain the cycle, and explaining the benign nature of intrusive thoughts is itself therapeutic. Normalising the phenomenon while treating the compulsions is what allows her to resume ordinary care of her baby. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence Australia)

options.text: Reassure her that these thoughts are common and review her in six weeks
options.rationale: Intrusive thoughts of harm genuinely do occur in a large majority of new parents and saying so is an important part of the consultation, but she has crossed from a normal phenomenon into a disorder because avoidance and checking are now restricting her behaviour. Reassurance without treatment leaves the compulsions to entrench. (Source: Centre of Perinatal Excellence Australia)

explanation.summary: Unwanted intrusive thoughts of harm coming to an infant are reported by the large majority of new mothers and fathers and are not in themselves pathological, which is why the threshold for disorder rests on distress, avoidance and compulsive behaviour rather than on the content of the thought. Perinatal obsessive compulsive disorder affects a few per cent of postpartum women and characteristically centres on contamination, checking and harm themes involving the baby. The critical safety distinction is between egodystonic obsessions, which the mother experiences as alien and repugnant and which carry no increased risk to the infant, and the ego syntonic thoughts of postpartum psychosis, which arise within a delusional framework and do carry serious risk. Getting this wrong in either direction is harmful: an unnecessary child protection referral drives concealment, while missing psychosis can be fatal. Women frequently take weeks to disclose these symptoms, so the disclosure itself should be met with normalisation before assessment continues.
key_points: Egodystonic intrusive thoughts are alien and repugnant and do not predict harm to the infant
Postpartum psychosis is distinguished by delusions, perceptual disturbance, disorientation or confusion
Avoidance and checking behaviour are what convert a normal intrusive thought into a disorder
Exposure and response prevention is the treatment, not an antipsychotic
Punitive responses to disclosure drive concealment in future pregnancies
explanation.pearls: Sertraline is the preferred serotonergic option if medication is added for perinatal obsessive compulsive disorder in a breastfeeding mother, because relative infant dose is low, and obsessive compulsive disorder needs the higher end of the dose range rather than the usual antidepressant dose.
